text:
Carrot.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Steady moisture, careful thinning and carrot-fly protection make a big difference. Fresh manure, compaction, stones, drought and rough handling can leave roots forked, tough or damaged.

Quick facts
Sow

Apr – Jun

Harvest

Aug – Oct

Germination

17 days

Sowing depth

1/2 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

early: 8 lb; maincrop: 10 lb

After thinning

2–3 in. between plants

Ready in

Early ~12; maincrop ~16 weeks from sowing

Extended season

Early: Mar under cloches. Late: Aug; cover against frost.

Recommended varieties
SHORT-ROOTED
Early Nantes 2

A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Autumn King

A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Chantenay Red Cored

A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

SHORT-ROOTED
Amsterdam Forcing

Early cylindrical roots with little core. Useful under cloches and for freezing.

Key risks
Carrot fly

Tell-tale signs on carrots are reddish leaves which wilt in sunny weather and later turn yellow.

Fanging

Stones, compaction, fresh manure or unfinished compost can fork roots. Properly used mature compost is suitable for no-dig carrots.

Small roots

Aphids and virus will stunt growth and reduce yield, but even in the absence of pests and diseases many gardeners produce disappointingly small carrots.

Splitting

Much more serious than fanging of carrots, because the roots will not store.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
36
ROOT CROPS

Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
Sow thinly
Cover lightly
Thin later
Sow 

Wait if the soil is cold or wet. Make shallow drills ½ in. deep and 6 in. apart, watering them first if dry. Sow very thinly; mixing the seed with dry sand can help. Cover with fine soil or compost and keep moist while the seeds germinate.

Extend the season 

Use short-rooted varieties for early or late crops. Early and later sowings need cloches or a sheltered spot.

Looking after the crop
Thin crowded seedlings to 2–3 in. apart in damp weather or in the evening. Water dry soil first, firm afterwards and clear the thinnings to avoid attracting carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.
Trim leaves about 1/2 in. above the crown. Store sound roots separately in sand, cool, ventilated and just above freezing; they may keep until March.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Carrot fly	Tunnelled roots.	Use fine mesh; remove thinnings; avoid bruising.
Fanging	Forked roots	Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.
Small roots	Small roots; weak growth.	Improve soil; use organic feed if growth is poor.
Splitting	Split roots.	Water evenly; mulch in drought; use split roots now.
Sclerotinia rot	White mould; rotting roots.	Remove diseased roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Carrot-willow aphid	Distorted, stunted leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Black rot	Black lesions on stored roots.	Remove rotten roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Motley dwarf virus	Yellow mottling; red outer leaves.	No cure; remove affected plants. Monitor aphids.
Final tips

Avoid fresh manure and disturbance around established roots.

Work from one end of the row when harvesting.

Inspect stored roots and remove any that rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
